cards.front: **The procurement cycle** — the eight-stage version
cards.back:
$$\textbf{Requirement Determination} \rightarrow \textbf{Source of Supply Determination} \rightarrow \textbf{Vendor Selection} \rightarrow \textbf{Order Processing}$$
$$\rightarrow \textbf{Purchase Order Monitoring} \rightarrow \textbf{Goods Receipt} \rightarrow \textbf{Invoice Verification} \rightarrow \textbf{Payment Processing}$$

**Read it as four questions:** *what do we need · who will supply it · order it and chase it · did it arrive and do we owe them.*

**Three of the eight stages are about settling up** — GR, invoice verification, payment. That is where the money moves and where the controls concentrate.

*(Shorter versions exist with 7 steps and 5 stages — the eight-stage diagram is the one to draw, since the others collapse out of it.)*

cards.front: **Three-way matching** — which three documents, and why three rather than two?
cards.back:
| Document | Created by | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Purchase Order** | **you** | *what did we agree to buy, at what price?* |
| **Goods Receipt** | **your warehouse** | *what actually arrived?* |
| **Invoice** | **the vendor** | *what are they charging us for?* |

**Match quantity against the GR; match price against the PO.** Fail either → **the invoice is blocked**.

> **Why three:** PO + invoice agreeing proves **nothing was delivered**. GR + invoice agreeing proves **nothing about the agreed price**. Only all three close both gaps.

**Separation of duties makes it work** — buyer raises the PO, storekeeper posts the GR, vendor sends the invoice. **No one person can create a payment for goods that never arrived.**

cards.front: **ERS — Evaluated Receipt Settlement**
cards.back:
**Pay the vendor from the GR and the PO alone — without waiting for an invoice.**

> **ERS is three-way matching with the third document deleted.**

If **PO price × GR quantity** already gives the correct amount, the invoice adds **no information** — only a document to type in and a chance of a mismatch. So remove it.

**What it costs:** total agreement on prices, and enough trust that neither party needs the invoice as evidence. **That is why it sits at level 2 of the maturity model, not level 1** — it is not a feature you switch on, it is a relationship you have to have first.

cards.front: **PR vs PO** — what is the difference?
cards.back:
| | **Purchase Requisition** | **Purchase Order** |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | **internal** — a request to your own purchasing dept | **external** — a request to the **vendor** |
| Commits the company? | **no** | **yes, legally** |
| Names a vendor? | not necessarily | **always** |

> **The PR is where a human approves; the PO is where money is committed.**

That is why **MRP produces requisitions, not orders** — *MRP proposes, a human confirms* — and why the approval workflow sits between them.

**PO definition:** *"a formal request/document to a vendor to supply certain goods or services under conditions stated in the order."* A **blanket PO** covers many deliveries over a long validity, used for **consumables** — same economics as lot sizing.

cards.front: **Contract types** — the two axes
cards.back:
| Axis | Types |
|---|---|
| **What it fixes** | **Quantity contract** *(10,000 units)* · **Value contract** *(₹50 lakh)* |
| **Who may release against it** | **Central / plant-independent** · **Plant specific** |

**Which unit you use depends on which side is predictable.** For **services** — where *"price comparison is complex"* — **value is the only meaningful unit.**

**Central contracts are how a multi-plant company buys as one company** — negotiate once at group volume, let every plant draw on it. *(The procurement answer to Nestlé's 29 vanilla records.)*

cards.front: **Quota arrangement** — why deliberately not buy everything from the cheapest vendor?
cards.back:
**A quota splits a material's requirement across approved vendors in fixed proportions** — *60% to A, 40% to B* — and the system allocates automatically.

**Three reasons to accept a higher average price:**
- **Supply risk** — a single source is a single point of failure
- **Negotiating position** — a vendor supplying 100% has all the leverage
- **Capacity** — no one vendor may be able to supply the whole volume

> **The quota is the price of not being hostage to one supplier.**

And ERP's contribution: **once the percentages are set, allocation happens without anyone deciding it order by order.**

cards.front: **Material vs service procurement** — the three differences and the four challenges
cards.back:
| **Material** | **Service** |
|---|---|
| **can be inventorized** | **cannot be inventorized** |
| **specifications clearly defined** | **difficult to define a service specification** |
| **price comparison is simple** | **price comparison is difficult** — *may differ by time of purchase, ambience* |

**Challenges of service procurement:** cannot be inventorized · difficult to specify · price comparison complex · **goods receipt is replaced by service entry and acceptance**

> **All four descend from one fact: a service does not exist as an object.**

$$\textbf{Service Entry Sheet} \rightarrow \textbf{Acceptance} \rightarrow \textbf{Invoice Verification}$$

**Acceptance is a judgement where goods receipt was a measurement** — which is why service procurement is harder to control.

cards.front: **Direct vs indirect items** — the six-row table
cards.back:
| | **Direct** | **Indirect** |
|---|---|---|
| **Demand** | driven by **end-item market demand** | **past consumption trend** |
| **Dept involvement** | **higher** — collaborate on component design | **lower** — off-the-shelf |
| **Share of spend** | **significant by value** | **small — low value items** |
| **Planning** | **MRP or APS** | **consumption based**; manual PRs |
| **Who procures** | **always the procurement team** | **also the end user**, via **E-Procurement / Portal** |
| **Back-end integration** | **higher** — delivery schedule releases | **lower** |

> **Direct items go into the product; indirect items keep the company running.**

**This is dependent vs independent demand:** direct = **MRP**, indirect = **CBP**.

cards.front: **Auctions vs hedging** — the two ERP tools for commodity procurement
cards.back:
| | **Auction** | **Hedging** |
|---|---|---|
| Problem solved | *what is the **best price right now**?* | *how do I stop **future price moves** hurting me?* |
| Market used | **physical** — real suppliers | **futures** — financial contracts |
| Effect | **discovers** the price | **fixes** the price |

> **Auction = price discovery. Hedging = price certainty.**

**Hedging:** *"taking a position in the futures market opposite to the one in the physical market."* You will **buy** copper, so a rise hurts → hold futures that **gain** when copper rises.

$$\textbf{physical loss} + \textbf{futures gain} \approx 0$$

**You have not made money — you have removed uncertainty.**

**A commodity is defined by being *not branded*** — so there is nothing to compete on except price.

cards.front: **The item strategy matrix** — four quadrants and their drivers
cards.back:
Plotted on **Strategic Impact** × **Financial Impact**:

| Item group | Position | **Driver** |
|---|---|---|
| **MRO** *(indirect goods/services)* | low / low | **"Purchase admin cost should be low"** |
| **Commodities** *(raw material)* | low strategic / **high financial** | **"Price is right"** |
| **Critical Items** *(spares)* | **high strategic** / low financial | **"Should never be out of stock"** |
| **Production Items** *(components)* | high / high | **"Need closer collaboration with vendor"** |

**The two axes are genuinely independent** — a commodity is a huge budget line but strategically dull; a critical spare costs ₹2,000 and stops the plant.

> **Read the matrix as a routing table**: each driver points to a different tool — blanket POs, auctions, safety stock, delivery schedules.

*(**MRO = Maintenance, Repair and Operation supplies**.)*

cards.front: **The procurement maturity model** — three levels
cards.back:
| Level | The vendor is… | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| **1 Basic** | **someone you send orders to** | basic planning, **mostly manual PRs & POs**, PO processes, vendor payment, GR, quality inspection |
| **2 Matured** | **someone you share information with** | **optimum planning (MRP/APS)**, **e-procurement**, **ERS**, **basic supplier collaboration** for forecast & inventory |
| **3 Innovative** | **someone you build products with** | **sourcing optimization**, **SRM**, **auctions and reverse auctions**, **advanced collaboration for product development**, **advanced supplier analytics**, exception management |

> **Transact → share → co-create.**

**The reliable test: does it need the vendor's cooperation?** If yes, level 2 or above.

⚠️ **E-procurement is level 2 but auctions are level 3** — buying through a portal is automation; running a competitive auction is a **strategy**.

cards.front: **Procurement master data and KPIs**
cards.back:
**Four master data objects — what · who · on-what-terms · services:**
**Material Master · Vendor Master · Terms and Conditions Master · Service Master / Service Catalog**

**Six KPIs, in three pairs:**

| Pair | KPIs |
|---|---|
| **Money** | **Cost Savings** · **Procurement ROI** *(savings ÷ operating costs)* |
| **Process** | **Procurement Cycle Time** *(requisition → PO)* · **Contract Compliance** |
| **Partners & spend** | **Supplier Performance** · **Purchasing Analysis** *(incl. ABC analysis)* |

> **Save · run · watch.**

**Cycle time stops at PO, not at delivery** — that is the part procurement controls. **A well-chosen KPI stops at the edge of the team's authority.**

cards.front: **The inventory management pyramid** — three levels and their annotation
cards.back:
$$\textbf{Transactions \& Inv Control (Lose)} \rightarrow \textbf{Inventory Planning (Maintain)} \rightarrow \textbf{Strategic IM (Gain)}$$

| Level | Contents |
|---|---|
| **Strategic Inventory Optimization** | deployment strategy · channel integration with suppliers · **VMI, CPFR, JIT, cross docking** |
| **Inventory Planning** | **inventory models** · quantitative determination of **safety stock, cycle stock, cost** |
| **Inventory Control** | record all transactions · **cycle counting** · tracking · **valuation** |

> **Accurate records are table stakes; strategy is advantage.**

⚠️ **The question bank asks for THREE levels** — the pyramid merges transactions and control into one base. *(The slide text elsewhere lists **four process groups** — same thing, different cut.)*

**Strictly dependent upward:** you cannot run a model on figures that are wrong.

cards.front: **The four inventory transaction processes**
cards.back:
| Process | Effect on stock |
|---|---|
| **Goods Receipt** | **in** |
| **Goods Issue** | **out** |
| **Stock Transfer** | **sideways** — total unchanged |
| **Reservations** | **none physically** — but the stock is **promised** |

> **In · out · sideways · spoken for.**

**GR:** ASN from supplier → receive → damage identification → unload/unpack → **capture lot #** → reconcile PO/schedule/GR → returns · **bar codes, RFID**

**GI:** create ASN to customer → pack and load → post → **receive POD**

> **Your goods issue is your customer's goods receipt** — the literal meaning of a supply *chain*.

⚠️ **Stock transfer "to Company" crosses a legal entity** — so it *is* a sale for accounting and tax, needing transfer pricing and consolidation elimination.

cards.front: **Cycle counting vs physical inventory**
cards.back:
| | **Physical inventory** | **Cycle counting** |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency | **once a year**, everything | **continuously**, a few items |
| Operations | **stop** | **carry on** |
| Error found after | **up to 12 months** | **days or weeks** |
| Effort allocation | **uniform** | **by ABC class** |

**Two wins:** errors surface **early**, and effort is allocated **by value rather than evenly**.

$$\textbf{count frequency} \propto \textbf{value at risk}$$

If **A items are 13.3% of items but 60.5% of value**, counting them monthly and C items annually **catches most of the error for a fraction of the effort.**

**Why control exists at all:** *"to match System Inv is a challenge"* — breakage, pilferage, mis-picks, unrecorded issues.

cards.front: **ABC classification** — the figures and the criterion
cards.back:
| Class | **% of value** | **% of items** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** *(very important)* | **60.5%** | **13.3%** |
| **B** *(moderately important)* | **25%** | **26.7%** |
| **C** *(least important)* | **14.5%** | **60%** |

**Criterion: annual value of *consumption*** — *consumption per period × price per unit*. **Not unit price alone.**

$$\underbrace{13.3\%}_{\text{of items}} \text{ carry } \underbrace{60.5\%}_{\text{of value}} \qquad \underbrace{60\%}_{\text{of items}} \text{ carry } \underbrace{14.5\%}_{\text{of value}}$$

**Roughly an order of magnitude difference in value-per-item** — Pareto, measured.

⚠️ **A cheap item consumed constantly can be class A; an expensive item bought once a year can be class C.**

cards.front: **The six inventory classification systems** *(image-only slide — no text layer)*
cards.back:
| Scheme | **Full form** | **Criterion** |
|---|---|---|
| **ABC** | **Always Better Control** | **Usage Value** *(consumption × price)* |
| **GOLF** | **Govt, ordinary, local, foreign** | **Source of procurement** |
| **SOS** | **Seasonal, off seasonal** | **Seasonality** |
| **HML** | **High, Medium, Low** | **Unit price — does NOT take consumption into account** |
| **FSND** | **Fast, slow, non-monetary, material demands** | **Issues from store** |
| **SDE** | **Scarce, difficult, easy** | **Procurement difficulties** |

**Six schemes, six different questions about the same item** — each serving a different department.

⚠️ **ABC vs HML is the pair most often confused** — the table itself flags it. **A gold-plated bolt bought twice a year is H under HML and C under ABC.**

*(Industry usually reads FSND as **FSN — Fast, Slow, Non-moving**; the criterion column is the reliable part. **Non-moving items are the obsolescence risk.**)*

cards.front: **Moving average price vs standard price**
cards.back:
| | **Moving average** | **Standard price** |
|---|---|---|
| Stock value | **recalculated on every receipt** | **fixed** at a planned price |
| Price differences | **absorbed into stock value** | **posted to a variance account** |
| Best for | **commodities** — genuinely variable costs | **production components** — stable costing |

**Standard price is what makes the price-variance posting exist:**
> **Inventory 245.00 · Goods Received 275.00 · Price Variance 30.00** — received at 275, valued at the standard 245, **30 to variance**.

**Why you want the variance:** product cost stays **comparable month to month**, and purchasing performance shows up **visibly** instead of being hidden inside the stock value.

*(Standard price lives in the **Material Master** — the Costing / Accounting view.)*

cards.front: **The four inventory models** — when and how much?
cards.back:
Every model answers two questions: **WHEN do we order?** and **HOW MUCH?**

| Model | **When** | **How much** |
|---|---|---|
| **Q model (EOQ)** | at the **reorder point** — *variable timing* | **fixed quantity** |
| **P model (periodic)** | at **fixed intervals** | **variable** — top up to target $M$ |
| **Min-max** | at **min** | up to **max** |
| **Two-bin** | **first bin empties** | **one bin's worth** |

> **Q fixes the quantity and lets timing float. P fixes the timing and lets quantity float.**

The deck states it: P is *"opposite of Q model — qty differs, freq is constant."*

**The practical argument for P is consolidation** — review every item from one vendor on the same day, place **one order, one delivery**. **Its cost:** P needs **more safety stock**, covering the review period *plus* the lead time.

cards.front: **EOQ and the reorder point** — the formulas and the reasoning
cards.back:
$$\textbf{Total annual cost} = \textbf{annual ordering cost} + \textbf{annual holding cost}$$

**Ordering cost** $\propto 1/Q$ — bigger lots, fewer orders, fixed cost spread thinner.
**Holding cost** $\propto Q$ — bigger lots, more average stock.

> **One falls, one rises — their sum has a minimum, and that is the EOQ.**

$$\textbf{Reorder Point} = \textbf{Daily Demand} \times \textbf{Lead Time} = D \times LT$$

**Reorder while you still have enough to survive the lead time.** 50/day × 6 days = **300**.

⚠️ **It assumes demand and lead time are certain.** Real systems add:
$$\textbf{ROP} = (D \times LT) + \textbf{safety stock}$$

cards.front: **The two drivers of inventory planning** — and why they conflict
cards.back:
**(i) Never have a stock out**
- finished goods → **customer dissatisfaction, lost sales**
- raw materials → **production loss**

**(ii) Never carry excess inventory**
- **increases cost of operation** · **chance of obsolescence** · **heavy markdown**

$$\textbf{Never stock out} \Rightarrow \text{hold more} \qquad \textbf{Never carry excess} \Rightarrow \text{hold less}$$

> **You cannot satisfy both, so the models exist to find the least-bad point.**

**"Heavy markdown" is the sharpest cost** — excess stock is eventually **sold below cost to clear it**, turning a working-capital problem into a realised loss.

**Same trade-off as Level vs Chase (S&OP) and central vs local stock (DRP).**

cards.front: **The four strategic inventory processes** — and what makes them "strategic"
cards.back:
1. **Inventory collaboration** — **VMI**; **Wal-Mart and P&G**
2. **Deciding inventory based on service levels** — *critical items, high service ⇒ high inventory*
3. **Best practices** — **cross docking** *(Wal-Mart; SAP, Oracle, Manhattan Associates)*
4. **Lean inventory management** — reduce waste, **Kanban or JIT**

> **Planning optimises within the rules; strategy changes the rules.**

| Process | What it changes |
|---|---|
| **VMI** | **who decides** the replenishment |
| **Service levels** | **the target itself** |
| **Cross docking** | **whether stock is held at all** |
| **Lean / JIT** | **how much waste the chain carries** |

**Nobody sets 100% service level** — that would need infinite stock. **Accepting some stock-outs is the correct policy.**

cards.front: **The nine inventory KPIs**
cards.back:
| Measure | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Stock outs** | # incidents of stock not available when required |
| **Inventory Turn** | **Annual sales / Average inventory level** |
| **Inventory Carrying Cost** | Σ all costs of finished goods |
| **SKU turnover** | # SKU cycles / turns |
| **Inventory Ageing** | Total gross inventory % for specific periods |
| **Cycle Counting Accuracy** | variance between physical and perpetual inventory |
| **Shrinkage** | **breakage, pilferage, deterioration** |
| **Storage space utilization** | volume of storage / total capacity, % |
| **Obsolescence % of Total Inventory** | obsolete & scrap / gross inventory value |

**Eight of the nine watch the *excess* side** — because **stock-outs are loud and excess inventory is silent.** You need instruments for the failure you cannot hear.

⚠️ **Shrinkage = what you lost. Cycle counting accuracy = how well you know what you have.** You can have low shrinkage and terrible accuracy — **and then the planning layer runs on wrong numbers.**

cards.front: **The 75–80% good-fit rule**
cards.back:
> **"No package will meet 100% of the company's needs. Objective is to find a package that is a good-fit (75–80% match) to business requirements and supports long term goals."**

**Why not 100%:** a package matching everything would have to be **built for you** — and then it is not a package. **The economics of ERP is shared development cost, which needs standard software.**

**Why not 50%:** the gap must be closed by **customization** (expensive, blocks upgrades) or **BPR** (which people resist).

$$\textbf{fit} \uparrow \Rightarrow \textbf{customization} \downarrow \text{ and } \textbf{organizational change} \downarrow$$

**Three named benefits:** lower user resistance · reduced training needs · less organizational adaptation.

**Gap analysis** = the gap between **process, data and user interface requirements** and **ERP offerings**.

cards.front: **The two-step selection process** — and why two steps
cards.back:
**Step 1 — Screening:** start with many packages, **shortlist two to a maximum of three** on a set of criteria.
**Step 2 — Final selection:** compare those two or three against **the list of requirements (100s)**, then contract.

$$\textbf{screening: many packages} \times \textbf{few criteria} \longrightarrow \textbf{selection: few packages} \times \textbf{many criteria}$$

> **Cheap criteria eliminate cheaply; expensive criteria are spent only on survivors.**

**Same economics as RCCP vs CRP and ABC-driven cycle counting** — match the cost of the check to the size of the remaining decision.

**Why the shortlist is 2–3:** small enough that detailed comparison is affordable; **large enough to retain negotiating leverage** right up to signature.

**Who:** a committee of **department heads plus CIO/CFO**, sometimes with consultants who know the packages.

cards.front: **The ten package selection criteria** — grouped
cards.back:
| Question | Criteria |
|---|---|
| **Does it do the job?** | **Functionality Fit · Industry Experience · Technology Maturity · Integration with 3rd party apps** |
| **Will the vendor still be here in ten years?** | **Financial Viability · Product Strategy & Vision · Installed Base · Partnerships** |
| **What will it cost, and who helps us?** | **Package Cost / TCO · Customer Service & Support · Local Presence · Consulting Partnerships** |

> **Fit · survival · support.**

**Roughly half concern the vendor as an institution, not the product** — because *"ERP package procurement is not a one-time transaction… help of the ERP vendor is needed throughout the package life cycle."*

**You are not buying a product; you are entering a decade-long dependency.**

cards.front: **Why financial viability and installed base matter** — with the deck's evidence
cards.back:
$$\textbf{JD Edwards, PeopleSoft, Siebel, Retek} \longrightarrow \textbf{Oracle}$$
$$\textbf{Manugistics} \longrightarrow \textbf{JD Edwards} \qquad \textbf{BAAN, Commerce One} \longrightarrow \textit{gone}$$

| Outcome | Consequence for you |
|---|---|
| **Vendor acquired** | product **merged, sunset or maintenance-only** |
| **Vendor fails** | **no support, patches or compliance updates** — on the system running your company |

> **The switching cost is what makes this catastrophic. Choosing the vendor is a lock-in decision, so vendor survival is a selection criterion.**

**Installed base is the evidence:** revenue, proven product, **available consultants**, and a customer base the vendor cannot abandon.

⚠️ **It must be the *relevant* base** — hence *geography specific, industry domain specific, MNC*.

cards.front: **TCO** and the **VED** requirement categories
cards.back:
**TCO = Total Cost of Ownership** = **initial capital + AMC + scaling # users**

**Two of the three are recurring** — so a package cheaper today can cost more over ten years.

⚠️ **The sharpest evaluation question on the deck's own list:** ***"Is the customization cost included in the ERP cost?"*** Almost always **no**.

---

**Final selection is a two-dimensional grid:**
$$\textbf{how well it matches} \times \textbf{how much that requirement matters}$$

| | **Full match** | **Partial** | **No match** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Vital** | fine | **serious problem** | **eliminate the package** |
| **Essential** | fine | manageable | costly gap |
| **Desirable** | bonus | fine | fine |

**A count of matches is misleading** — 900 of 1,000 looks excellent until one of the misses is **Vital**.

cards.front: **Why companies skip the traditional selection process** — four reasons
cards.back:
1. **Pressure from major customers** to be on their platform
2. **Same ERP for all companies in the group** — integration and consolidation
3. **Price dominant** — especially for **SMB**
4. **Industry specific functionality**

> **Three of the four are perfectly rational: a constraint outside the evaluation outweighs everything inside it.**

**Reason 2 is the direct answer to Nestlé** — nine general ledgers arose because divisions chose independently. **Standardising the package is how a group stops that recurring.**

⚠️ **Reason 4 is better described as one criterion dominating all others** — *industry experience* IS one of the criteria. When only one package supports your industry's core process, the weighted comparison has one possible outcome.

cards.front: **The ERP vendor contract** — the ten clauses, and the three that hurt if omitted
cards.back:
**Payment terms · IP/copyright · deliverables · training · maintenance · upgrades and their cost · installation help · prerequisites (hardware, OS, database) · vendor audits · licence cancellation costs**

| When they bite | Clauses |
|---|---|
| **At purchase** | payment · deliverables · IP |
| **During implementation** | installation · prerequisites · training · **vendor audits** |
| **For years after** | maintenance · **upgrades and cost** |
| **At the end** | **licence cancellation** |

**Only three of ten concern the purchase itself.**

⚠️ **The three that hurt:** **upgrade cost** *(no price protection = a negotiation you cannot walk away from)*; **licence cancellation** *(negotiate the exit while you still have leverage)*; **vendor audits** — *final blueprint audit* and *audit before go live*, which are **the vendor checking YOUR implementation**, and you want that agreed in advance.

cards.front: **The three ERP package market tiers**
cards.back:
| Tier | Players | Typical customer |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **SAP, Oracle** | **large enterprises, MNCs, multi-country** |
| **2** | **Microsoft Dynamics, JD Edwards, PeopleSoft, Infor, IFS, Epicor, Lawson, QAD** | **mid-market, large single-country** |
| **3** | **small and local players** | **small businesses** |

> **Tiers segment by customer size, not by quality.**

**A Tier 1 package is frequently the wrong choice for a small company** — *price becomes the dominant factor for SMB*, and TCO grows with the tier. **The reverse also holds:** Tier 3 will not support multi-country statutory reporting.

**Evidence, from the image-only comparison table:** industry-specific software — **SAP 25 industries · Oracle 23 · Microsoft Dynamics AX 4.** **Breadth of industry coverage is what Tier 1 is selling.**

cards.front: **Preconfigured templates** — why they exist for SMBs
cards.back:
**A package that arrives already configured for a typical company in an industry** — chart of accounts, org structure, standard processes — instead of a blank system.

**Configuration effort is roughly fixed; its value scales with company size:**

$$\text{large firm: } \frac{\text{config cost}}{\text{benefit}} \text{ small} \qquad \text{small firm: } \frac{\text{config cost}}{\text{benefit}} \text{ large}$$

> **The template collapses that ratio by making configuration a product rather than a project.**

**What you give up is choice** — it embeds *someone else's* view of the process. **Fine for an SMB with no strong opinion; unacceptable where the process is the competitive advantage.**

**The idea returns in Unit 5:** industry best-practice configurations are the enabling condition for **SaaS ERP**, where customization is forbidden outright.

cards.front: **The ten consulting partner selection criteria** — and how they differ from package criteria
cards.back:
**Industry Experience · Process Consulting Experience · Client Reference & Satisfaction · End-to-End Service · Quality of Project Management · Quality of Tools and Methodologies · Presence in Different Geographies · Global Delivery Capability · Reputation and Branding · Price and Value for Money**

> **Know · work · reach · reputation.**

| | **Package criteria** | **Partner criteria** |
|---|---|---|
| Dominant concern | **will the vendor survive?** | **can these people deliver?** |

**You buy a package for a decade, so you assess the vendor as an institution. You buy a partner for a project, so you assess capability to execute.**

⚠️ **"Presence in different geographies" ≠ "global delivery capability"** — being in many places is not the same as being able to **work across** them.

cards.front: **The RFP process** — steps, and the three details that matter
cards.back:
**RFI (optional) → RFP Preparation → RFP Release *(conference call · common meeting · media advertisement)* → Response Collection → Evaluation → Partner Selection → Contract Negotiations → Partner Finalization → Contract Signing → Kick off**

**① RFI shortlists; RFP selects** — the same screening-then-selection economics as package selection.

**② Release is not just sending the document** — conference call and common meeting exist so **every bidder hears the same clarifications**; media advertisement makes the process **open**, which is why it is mandatory in the public sector.

**③ Selection and finalization are separate, with negotiation between:**
$$\textbf{Selection} \rightarrow \textbf{Negotiations} \rightarrow \textbf{Finalization} \rightarrow \textbf{Signing}$$
**If negotiations fail you can still turn to the runner-up.**

**Bids are evaluated on two dimensions: Technical and Financial** — clear the technical bar first, compete on price second.

cards.front: **In-house vs external implementation**
cards.back:
| **In-house has** | **External has** |
|---|---|
| **better process knowledge** | **product expertise** |
| **better industry knowledge** | **methods and tools** |
| *"no money goes outside"* | **implementation experience** · **ERP project management skill** |

**Cons of in-house:** lack of methods and tools · no implementation experience · **high chances of failure** · *"implementation is not their core competency"* · **"may not be cost effective if all internal costs are factored"**

⚠️ **The deck contradicts its own "no money goes outside" pro** — and that IS the point. **The saving is visible (no invoice); the cost is invisible** (senior staff off their day jobs, longer timeline, rework).

> **Where it works: ROLLOUTS** — consultants proved the template at site one, so site two is **repetition, not design**.

cards.front: **The phase-wise offshoring table** — and the rule behind it
cards.back:
| Phase | **On-site** | **Offshore** | Offshored activity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Project Preparation** | **100%** | **0%** | — |
| **Business Blueprint** | 90% | **10%** | PoC / demo scenarios, partial documentation |
| **Realization** | 30% | **70%** | **configuration, testing, development** |
| **Final Prep & Go Live** | 50% | **50%** | data migration, training content |
| **Support** | 20% | **80%** | issue resolution, utility jobs, change requests |

$$\textbf{offshore \%} \propto \frac{1}{\textbf{customer contact required}}$$

> **Work that is *specified* can be offshored; work that is *discovered* cannot.**

**The dip at Go Live** (70% → 50%) is because go-live needs **training, hand-holding and physical presence**.

**Difficult to offshore:** blueprinting · **integration testing** · **UAT** · end user training · change management. *(**Unit testing IS offshorable** — that split is examinable.)*

**ODC** = Offshore Development Center · **GDC** = Global Delivery Center

cards.front: **The nine levers of ERP project scope**
cards.back:
| Lever | The question |
|---|---|
| **Location** | which **sites, plants, countries**? |
| **Business** | which **legal entities / business units**? |
| **Process** | which **business processes** — P2P, O2C, H2R? |
| **Application** | which **modules** — FI, MM, SD, PP, HR? |
| **Interface** | which **other systems**? |
| **Report** | which **reports**? |
| **Data Migration** | which **data objects**, and how much history? |
| **User** | **how many users**, which roles? |
| **Technology** | which **platform, OS, database, landscape**? |

> **A lever is something you can pull to make the project bigger or smaller.** When over budget you have **nine choices, not nine hundred**.

**The instruction is the point:** *"identify in-scope and **out-of-scope** items clearly (and get sign off)."* **An unstated exclusion is an assumed inclusion.**

⚠️ **Process scope is horizontal; application scope is vertical.** Scope by process, verify by application.

cards.front: **Data migration objects** — master vs transaction, and the principle
cards.back:
**Master data objects:** Material · Customer · Vendor · Asset · **Chart of Accounts** · Cost/Profit Centres & Cost Elements · Pricing Condition · **BOM, Routing, Work Centres** · Plant Maintenance · Quality Management · Warehouse

**Transaction data objects:** **GL balances & open items** · customer **open** items · vendor **open** items · budget values · loans and advances · **open** internal orders · stock balances · **material in transit (high seas, on port)** · **open** service contracts & orders · **open** contracts & POs · **open** sales contracts & orders

> **The word "open" appears seven times, and it is the whole principle.**

$$\textbf{migrate} = \textbf{the state the business is in}, \text{ not } \textbf{the story of how it got there}$$

**Master data can be loaded weeks ahead; open transaction data only at the last moment** — which is why **cutover** is its own minutely-planned phase.

cards.front: **The six component plans**, and where the resource plan comes from
cards.back:
1. **Activity, Deliverables and Milestone plan**
2. **Resource plan**
3. **Training Plan**
4. **Testing Plan**
5. **Data Migration Plan**
6. **Change Management Plan**

**Five of the six are named after the things that most often go wrong** — *lack of planning* (39%), *inadequate co-ordination of resources* (26%), *no quality control* (34%), *clean data*, *inadequate change management*.

**Resource plan has four dimensions:** **when** (month) · **where** (site or offshore) · **whose** (consulting or core team) · **ramp up / ramp down**.

> **"Resource Plan is derived from Project Plan"** — you plan the work, then compute the people. **Staffing to availability rather than to plan is how *aggressive time frame* becomes unachievable.**

cards.front: **The project charter** — what it fixes, and the section that carries most weight
cards.back:
A **major deliverable of Project Preparation**, presented formally at the **Kick Off Meeting**.

| Section | Fixes |
|---|---|
| overview, business case, benefits | **why** |
| scope, deliverables, goals | **what** |
| stakeholders, organisation and roles | **who decides** |
| implementation strategy, plan, standards | **how** |
| **assumptions, constraints, risk assessment** | **what could go wrong** |

> **"Assumptions and Constraints" carries the most weight in practice.**

Every estimate rests on assumptions — *the data is clean*, *the core team is full-time*. **Writing them down converts a later argument ("you should have known") into a fact ("this assumption failed, here is the impact").**

**Milestones must be *completed deliverables*, not dates:** *"to-be design **completed**"*, not *"blueprinting going well."*

cards.front: **Risk impact levels and the five-step approach**
cards.back:
| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Negligible** | minor inconvenience |
| **Marginal** | degradation of **secondary** mission |
| **Critical** | serious threat to **primary objective** |
| **Catastrophic** | **failure of primary mission** |

> **"Identify all critical and catastrophic threats and deal with them proactively"** — you are explicitly told **not** to actively mitigate the lower two.

**Five steps:** find risks → **assess probability** → **analyze impact** → prioritize → **mitigate the TOP risks**

$$\textbf{risk exposure} \approx \textbf{probability} \times \textbf{impact}$$

**Steps 2 and 3 are separate because neither factor alone tells you what to do.**

**Mitigation remedies named:** appropriate selection team · right selection process · adequate budget · adequate time. **Three of four are "do not rush the selection."**

cards.front: **The three-tier risk taxonomy** *(image-only slide)*
cards.back:
$$\textbf{every project} \subset \textbf{technology project} \subset \textbf{ERP project}$$

**Every project:** low user involvement · poor project team skills · low top management support · poor project monitoring · ineffective PM techniques · scarcity of resources · changing external environment · **attrition**

**Technology project:** inadequate management of IT issues · **scope creep** · volatile IT system · instable vendor

**ERP project:** implementation strategy · **inadequate selection** · ineffective communication system · **inadequate change management** · ineffective vendor and consultant · inadequate training · **inadequate BPR** · inappropriate implementation strategy · complexity of the ERP system · **inadequate legacy system management**

> **An ERP project carries all twenty-two, not just its own ten** — which is why they fail more often.

**Nine of the ten ERP-specific risks are things this course teaches you to prevent.** Only *"complexity of the ERP system"* is inherent.

cards.front: **The four fundamentals of requirements management**
cards.back:
1. **Granularity depends on the organization** — and on what level it is defined at
2. **"Requirements mean different things to different people"** — state them clearly
3. **Requirement should be verifiable**
4. **Prioritization is important**

> **③ is the strongest: a requirement you cannot test cannot be accepted or rejected** — so it gets argued about at UAT, when it is most expensive.

| Not verifiable | Verifiable |
|---|---|
| *"must be user friendly"* | *"a GR postable in under 6 keystrokes"* |
| *"reports should be fast"* | *"stock overview returns in under 5 seconds"* |

**Five requirement types:** **Business · Functional · Legal · User · Maintainability**

**Legal requirements are automatically Vital** — you cannot descope a statutory return. **Maintainability is the one teams forget**, and forgetting it is how you get *"customizing the software too much."*

cards.front: **The two-team structure and the core team's five responsibilities**
cards.back:
**Consulting team brings product knowledge and implementation experience; core team brings business knowledge.** *"Successful knowledge transfer from each other only ensures that the project is successful."*

**Core team responsibilities:**
1. **Business inputs during TO-BE process design**
2. **Configuring the system**
3. **Validation of data before loading**
4. **Testing**
5. **Training end users — using Train the Trainer**

**Each exists because only the business side can do it** — only they know a genuine duplicate from two real customers; only they know what a correct result looks like.

**Train the Trainer:** consultants train the core team, the core team trains the end users. **It scales, transfers ownership, and leaves the knowledge inside the company.**

⚠️ ***"For projects to succeed the core team need to be full time"*** — the success factor most often violated.

cards.front: **The ranked failure percentages** — and the annotation that matters
cards.back:
| Reason | % |
|---|---|
| **Poor communication between relevant parties** | **57%** |
| **Lack of planning of scheduling, resources and activities** | **39%** |
| **No quality control** | **34%** |
| **Milestones not being set** | **29%** |
| **Inadequate co-ordination of resources** | **26%** |
| **Costs getting out of hand** *(**a symptom not a cause**)* | **20%** |
| **Mismanagement of progress** *(overlaps with communication)* | **17%** |
| Overall poor management · suppliers overstretched · supplier under-resourced | 13% · 12% · 11% |

**① Communication leads by a wide margin — the #1 cause of ERP failure is not technical.**

**② "Costs getting out of hand" is flagged as a symptom** — costs rise *because* scope changed or rework was needed. **Treating the overrun as the problem leads to cutting testing and training, which makes the real causes worse.**

$$\underbrace{\text{top five}}_{\textbf{generic project management}} \gg \underbrace{\text{supplier problems}}_{\text{12\% + 11\%}}$$

cards.front: **Success and failure are the same list with the signs flipped** — show it
cards.back:
| Success factor | Failure twin |
|---|---|
| well-thought package selection | **poor ERP package selection** |
| realistic documented expectations | **unrealistic expectations** |
| proper ROI justification | **investment without ROI justification** |
| top management support | **top management support lacking** |
| best brains with the consultants | **core team lacks right resource** |
| **user acceptance** | **user acceptance issues** |
| handling employee resistance | **employees resist** |
| training at every level | **training issues** |
| **communication** | **poor communication** |
| **business project, not IT project** | **project viewed as an IT project** |
| **minimize customization** | **customizing too much** |
| adequate time per activity | **too tight schedule** |
| **full-time core team** | **high turnover of team members** |

> **There is no separate theory of failure: projects fail by the absence of the things that make them succeed.**

**The most quotable line:** *"**without user acceptance, even if the system goes LIVE, it will never be used by end users.**"* **Go-live is not success.**

cards.front: **The four documented ERP failures**
cards.back:
| Company | Package / Partner | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| **W. L. Gore** | **PeopleSoft** / **Deloitte & Touche** | Oct 1997 live; **faulty. "Deloitte & Touche not experts"** |
| **FoxMeyer Drug Co.** | **SAP America** / **Anderson Consulting** | **Bankruptcy 1998** — *"could not handle the huge volume of transactions; integration problems"* |
| **Cleveland State University** | **PeopleSoft** / **Kaludis Consulting** | *"full of bugs; extra hardware"* |
| **Hershey** | **SAP R/3, 1999** / **IBM** | *"bugs"* |

> **Every case names a Tier 1 package and a Tier 1–2 firm. Choosing famous names is not a defence.**

**FoxMeyer is the one to know in detail** — a drug distributor's business *is* high-volume transaction processing, so a system that cannot process the volume is **no system**. **Catastrophic: failure of primary mission.**

**Hershey's 1999 go-live near peak season** is the cutover-timing cautionary tale.

cards.front: **The change request process and the three-environment cycle**
cards.back:
1. **User requests a change**
2. **Impact analyzed and change approved**
3. **Made in DEVELOPMENT, transported to QUALITY**
4. **All documents (process and config) updated**
5. **Tested in quality, transported to PRODUCTION**

$$\textbf{Development} \xrightarrow{\textbf{Approval}} \textbf{Test} \xrightarrow{\textbf{Approval}} \textbf{Production}$$

| Environment | Why separate |
|---|---|
| **Development** | mistakes must be **free** |
| **Quality / Test** | testing needs **stable, complete** data |
| **Production** | **nothing untested may ever touch it** |

**"Transported" is precise** — the same object moves forward, so **what was tested is exactly what goes live**.

⚠️ **Step 4 comes BEFORE the final transport. Documentation is a precondition for going live, not a follow-up task.**

**Three needs for change:** a **vendor patch** (outside) · a **new business requirement** (inside) · **continuous improvement** (from operating it).

cards.front: **Cutover and go-live**
cards.back:
**Cutover** — *"the final stage of ERP Realization before the company moves on to the new system."* Transactions stop in the old system briefly and move to the new one.

> **It is important to understand the criticality of the transaction before planning the cutover.**

**Customer ordering and invoicing** must not stop — **revenue loss**. **Maintenance orders and new purchase contracts** can be deferred a week.

⚠️ **"Typically every department believes their transactions are most critical"** — so it **must be a senior management decision**.

---

**Go Live** — the day you move off the legacy system.

$$\textbf{go-live criterion} = \textbf{zero critical open items} + \textbf{a dated closure plan for the rest}$$

**"It's OK to have such issues"** — waiting for zero means never going live. But **an undocumented open issue is a defect that has been forgotten.**

**Go Live audit:** integration testing · training · **UAT signoff** · data migration · **support help desk** · period-end procedures · critical open items. **Five of seven are readiness, not correctness.**

cards.front: **SLA parameters and priority levels**
cards.back:
**Service Contract** = a long-term agreement specifying services for a period.
**SLA** = *"contracts that assure the customer performance of certain services within a predefined period of time."*

| Measures | Parameters |
|---|---|
| **How reliable is the system?** | **Downtime** *(breakdowns/year)* · **Availability** *(% uptime)* |
| **How responsive is support?** | **Response time** · **Service window** · **Solution time** |

⚠️ **Response time and solution time are deliberately separate.** *"We called back in 15 minutes"* satisfies response while the problem stays unsolved for a week. **An SLA with response time and no solution time is much weaker than it looks.**

**P1/P2 → 24×7 on call, on rotation. P3/P4 → next business day.**

**Service Level Reports (SLR)** monthly check adherence — *"how you define success: define measures"* applied to the support phase.

cards.front: **Why heavy customization eventually forces a replacement**
cards.back:
> ***"If a large amount of customization has taken place, the ERP system may not be able to evolve. It is a strong indicator for the organization to start looking for an alternative."***

$$\textbf{customization} \uparrow \Rightarrow \textbf{upgrade cost} \uparrow \Rightarrow \textbf{upgrades stop} \Rightarrow \textbf{system frozen} \Rightarrow \textbf{replace it}$$

**The mechanism:** every vendor upgrade must be re-tested against every modification, and modifications break as the standard code changes. Past a threshold, **upgrading costs more than it is worth** — so you stop, and the system stops receiving **statutory updates, security patches and new functionality.**

**It slowly becomes the legacy system you replaced.**

> **That closes the loop back to the 75–80% good-fit rule** — which avoided the customization that would have forced this outcome.

**Preparedness for the future** needs three things to keep up: **your people (trained), the system, and the vendor.**
